waveform.note: The first 2 seconds of each condition, keeping one sample in 2. Values are recorded microvolt readings.

recordings: EEG across the scalp, summarized as absolute power in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands in 9 scalp regions.
Skin conductance level, as an index of arousal.
study.protocol: Participants sat at rest with no task, once with the eyes closed and once with them open. Both are common baselines for other studies, and they differ in visual input and in arousal.
findings: Skin conductance level rose from eyes closed to eyes open.
With the eyes closed, people with higher skin conductance had lower mean alpha.
Mean power across the scalp fell in all four bands when the eyes opened.
Alpha fell evenly across the scalp. The other bands changed in specific places, such as lower posterior theta and lower posterior, higher frontal beta with the eyes open.
study.interpretation: The authors read the even drop in alpha as a change in overall arousal, and the local changes in other bands as the brain processing visual input. Eyes-closed and eyes-open baselines therefore differ in more than alpha, and a study should choose between them on purpose.

ageing.participants: 20 young adults (mean age 20.4) and 20 older adults (mean age 68.2).
ageing.protocol: Eyes closed first, then eyes open.
findings: Older adults showed some reduction in alpha.
Power in all bands dropped when the eyes opened, by similar amounts at both ages.
Older adults showed more local changes, especially in beta.
ageing.interpretation: The eyes-closed to eyes-open change holds in healthy ageing, which matters here: the recording in this journey comes from a woman aged 60 to 80, a different person and dataset from either study.

measures.name: Frequency
measures.what_it_is: How many times per second a rhythm repeats.
measures.how_computed: The recording is split into frequency components. Alpha here is everything from 8 to 13 Hz.
measures.how_to_read: A higher number means a faster rhythm. Bands are named ranges of frequency.
measures.expected: The 8 to 13 Hz alpha band is a convention. Each person's alpha peak sits somewhere inside or near it.
measures.what_shifts_it: Age and scalp position. Alpha frequency rises through childhood and slows in older adults, and it runs faster over the back of the head. Many people show more than one alpha peak.

measures.name: Voltage
measures.what_it_is: The electrical potential at one electrode, measured against a reference electrode.
measures.how_computed: The amplifier samples it 500 times per second. Each sample is one number.
measures.how_to_read: Larger swings mean more synchronized activity near that electrode. Timing matters as much as numbers: neurons firing out of step cancel each other at the scalp. The sign depends on the reference.
measures.expected: Compare conditions within one recording. Absolute voltages change with the reference, the amplifier, and the person.
measures.what_shifts_it: The reference electrode, skull and scalp thickness, electrode contact, filtering, and movement or blink artifacts.

measures.name: Alpha power
measures.what_it_is: How strong the 8 to 13 Hz rhythm is in one second of signal.
measures.how_computed: Each 1-second window (500 samples) gets one Hann-windowed power spectrum, using Welch's method with a single segment, so there is no overlap or averaging. The spectrum has 1 Hz steps. Alpha power is the area under it from 8 to 13 Hz. Power comes from squared voltage, which is why the unit is µV².
measures.how_to_read: Higher means a stronger alpha rhythm in that second. Each dot on the strip is one second.
measures.expected: Read it within a person, across conditions. Absolute alpha power has no single normal value.
measures.what_shifts_it: Age, scalp position, the reference electrode, the device, and arousal. Alpha power is higher over the back of the head and differs between the sexes.

measures.name: Eyes-closed to eyes-open ratio
measures.what_it_is: Mean alpha power with the eyes closed divided by mean alpha power with them open.
measures.how_computed: Average the eyes-closed windows, average the eyes-open windows, and divide.
measures.how_to_read: Above 1 means alpha was stronger with the eyes closed. A value of 1 means no difference.
measures.expected: Above 1 is the expected direction in relaxed, awake adults, young and older. How far above 1 varies from person to person.
measures.what_shifts_it: Drowsiness, arousal, attention, age, and scalp position.

measures.name: Accuracy against chance
measures.what_it_is: How often the threshold rule labeled a second as eyes closed or eyes open correctly.
measures.how_computed: Each second is labeled eyes closed when its alpha power is above a threshold, set at the midpoint of the two condition means. Accuracy is correct windows divided by all windows.
measures.how_to_read: With equal numbers of each condition, guessing gets 50% on average. A small sample can beat 50% by luck, so the bar to clear depends on how many windows there are.
measures.expected: Chance is 50% by design. For 30 windows, 20 correct (67%) is the smallest count that luck alone reaches less than 5% of the time.
measures.what_shifts_it: The number of windows, how the threshold was set, and whether it was tested on separate data.

measures.name: Skin conductance level
measures.what_it_is: How easily a small current passes between two electrodes on the skin, which rises with sweat gland activity.
measures.how_computed: Two electrodes, often on the fingers, with a small constant voltage between them. The recording in this journey has no skin conductance channel.
measures.how_to_read: Higher means more sympathetic arousal. A slow level (tonic) and quick responses to events (phasic) are read separately.
measures.expected: Barry et al. (2007) found it rises from eyes closed to eyes open. Absolute levels vary widely between people and setups, so studies compare within a person.
measures.what_shifts_it: Temperature, electrode site and gel, hydration, medication, and exercise.

bands.name: Theta
bands.plain: Linked with encoding new information during memory tasks.

bands.name: Alpha
bands.plain: Strongest in relaxed wakefulness with the eyes closed.

resting_state.band_caveat: Band edges are conventions that vary by about 1 Hz between labs. Anchoring each band on a person's own alpha peak can be more accurate.

dichotomies.first: Eyes-closed and eyes-open rest, with no task.
dichotomies.second: A memory task, where alpha drops briefly (phasic) in response to each item.

dichotomies.first: Alpha falling evenly across the scalp, read as overall arousal.
dichotomies.second: Theta and beta changing over specific regions, read as visual processing.

dichotomies.first: Resting-state scans, where slow fluctuations below 0.1 Hz rise and fall together in connected regions.
dichotomies.second: Task scans, where goal-directed work engages task regions and quiets the default mode network.

dichotomies.first: Frontal and parietal regions that respond across many demanding tasks, from arithmetic to working memory.
dichotomies.second: Neighboring regions that respond to one kind of content.

dichotomies.first: The slow tonic level across a resting condition.
dichotomies.second: Quick phasic responses to individual events.

dichotomies.first: Sympathetic arousal shared by emotion, attention, and effort.
dichotomies.second: A specific reading needs a task or another signal alongside it, because the same rise accompanies emotion, attention, and effort.

threshold.text: The threshold is the midpoint of the two condition means in this recording: (77.8 + 9.2) / 2 = 43.5 µV². It fits this recording only, and another person or device would need its own. It was set from the same windows it labels, so accuracy on new data would likely be lower.

steps.title: Why square the signal?
steps.question: A rhythm can be strong, yet its average voltage is zero. How do we measure its strength?
steps.explanation: Over each cycle, the positive half and the negative half cancel, so the mean voltage stays at zero whatever the amplitude. Squaring makes every sample positive, so both halves add up. For a sine of amplitude A, the mean square is A² / 2.
steps.takeaway: Power is the mean of the squared signal. That is why its unit is µV².

steps.title: Why split the signal into frequencies?
steps.question: Real EEG mixes several rhythms and noise. How do we measure only the alpha rhythm?
steps.explanation: Fourier analysis splits a signal into sine waves of different frequencies. The power spectral density shows how the mean square is shared among them. Raise the alpha amplitude: the waveform barely changes to the eye, while the 8 to 13 Hz part of the spectrum grows and the rest stays put.
steps.takeaway: The spectrum separates rhythms that overlap in time.

steps.title: Why add up the area from 8 to 13 Hz?
steps.question: How does a spectrum become one number for one second of recording?
steps.explanation: Each point of the spectrum is power per hertz. Adding up the area between 8 and 13 Hz gives the power that belongs to the alpha band, in µV². The whole area equals the window's mean square after the Hann taper, which weighs the middle of the second more than its edges. For a steady signal that matches the plain mean square on average. Real EEG changes within a second, so here the two can differ.
steps.takeaway: Alpha power is the alpha band's share of the window's mean square.

downsample.failure: sampling_rate=12.5 Hz cannot resolve the 8.0-13.0 Hz alpha band: its Nyquist frequency (6.25 Hz) is at or below the band's lower edge.

systems.name: Frontal lobe
systems.location: Front of the brain, behind the forehead
systems.role: Planning, attention, decision making, and control of behavior.

systems.name: Primary motor and sensory cortex
systems.location: A strip over the top of the brain, on both sides of the central sulcus
systems.role: The primary motor cortex, in front of the sulcus, sends movement commands. The primary sensory cortex, behind it, receives touch and body position. Planning a movement also draws on wider frontal and parietal areas. Motor imagery brain computer interfaces read rhythms over this strip.

systems.name: Parietal lobe
systems.location: Top and back of the brain
systems.role: Combines touch, vision, and body position to guide attention and movement in space.

systems.name: Temporal lobe
systems.location: Side of the brain, above the ear
systems.role: Hearing, language comprehension, and recognizing objects and faces.

systems.name: Occipital lobe (visual cortex)
systems.role: Processes vision. In relaxed, awake adults, scalp alpha is usually strongest over occipital and parietal sites with the eyes closed. Its generators are distributed across cortical and thalamocortical networks, so no single patch of cortex produces it.

systems.name: Thalamus
systems.location: Center of the brain, above the brainstem
systems.role: Relays sensory signals to the cortex and takes part in the thalamocortical loops that shape rhythms such as alpha.

systems.name: Hippocampus and amygdala
systems.role: Forms new memories (hippocampus) and processes emotion and threat (amygdala).

systems.name: Cerebellum
systems.location: Below the occipital lobe, at the back of the head
systems.role: Coordinates and times movement and supports motor learning.

systems.name: Brainstem
systems.location: Base of the brain, where it joins the spinal cord
systems.role: Regulates heart rate, breathing, and arousal, and links the brain to the body.

systems.name: Autonomic nervous system
systems.location: Nerves from the brainstem and spinal cord to the heart, skin, and organs
systems.role: Adjusts heart rate, sweating, and pupil size without conscious control.

modalities.name: Scalp electroencephalography
modalities.configuration: A whole-head cap of scalp electrodes. This journey uses one of its channels, O1.
modalities.measures: Voltage differences between each electrode and a reference.
modalities.neural_link: Direct electrical measure: mostly summed postsynaptic currents of cortical pyramidal neurons firing in step.
modalities.timing: Milliseconds. Fast enough to follow each cycle of the 8 to 13 Hz alpha rhythm.

modalities.name: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy
modalities.configuration: A forehead array of light sources and detectors, a common wearable layout. Optodes placed elsewhere on the head cover the cortex beneath them instead.
modalities.measures: Changes in oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin, from how much near-infrared light returns to each detector.
modalities.neural_link: Indirect: blood oxygen changes that follow neural activity, mixed with scalp blood flow and changes across the whole body.
modalities.timing: Seconds. Blood flow follows neural activity with a delay.

modalities.also_captures: The face. Face recognition software matched MRI face reconstructions to photographs for 70 of 84 research participants (83%) as the top match, and for 80 of 84 (95%) within the top five.
modalities.privacy_note: Removing the face before sharing, called defacing, lowers this risk. In a later study, face recognition matched 97% of 157 scans before defacing, and 28 to 38% still matched after popular defacing tools.

modalities.name: Peripheral body sensors (skin conductance and heart rate)
modalities.configuration: Sensors on the skin, wrist, or chest.
modalities.measures: Sweat gland activity and the timing of each heartbeat.
modalities.neural_link: No brain region is measured. These signals reflect the autonomic nervous system's effects on skin and heart.
modalities.timing: Seconds for skin conductance. Every beat for heart rate.

coverage.note: Body responses carry traces of brainstem control. Reading those traces is inference from another signal.
Measured through its effects on skin and heart.

modalities.also_captures: Signs of autonomic arousal. Exercise, temperature, medication, and illness change these signals too, so neither one measures stress by itself.
modalities.privacy_note: Common in consumer wearables, so these signals are often collected far outside research settings.

neuroanatomy.electrode_caveat: An electrode records the voltage difference between its site and a reference. Currents spread through tissue (volume conduction), so each electrode picks up a blend of sources, with nearby cortex contributing most. The glow around O1 is schematic.
neuroanatomy.caveat: Schematic drawing: region shapes and boundaries are approximate. Coverage levels are teaching simplifications for the configuration described, drawn from the cited reviews. Real coverage depends on how many sensors there are, where they sit, signal quality, and how the data are analyzed. Shading shows where a signal comes from, and its color shows what kind of signal it is.
